content: 1. Neonatal resuscitation does not require slapping the infant. Instead, rubbing the back two or three times, combined with thorough drying, is sufficient for stimulation. 2. To open the airway, position the infant's head slightly extended. Routine suctioning is not recommended. Suction the airway only if there is meconium-stained fluid and the infant is not crying or moving limbs. If the amniotic fluid is clear, suction only if the nose or mouth is full of secretions. Suction the mouth, nose, and oropharynx under direct vision, avoiding deep suctioning down the throat to prevent apnea or bradycardia. 3. For infants weighing less than 5 kg, ventilate using a bag and mask at a rate of 40–60 breaths per minute. Ensure the chest rises with each bag compression, but avoid excessive chest movement in very small infants to prevent pneumothorax. 4. If the heart rate remains below 60 beats per minute after 30–60 seconds of effective ventilation with adequate chest movement, initiate chest compressions. Perform 90 compressions coordinated with 30 breaths per minute (three compressions to one breath every two seconds). Place thumbs just below the line connecting the nipples on the sternum and compress one-third of the chest's anterior-posterior diameter. 5. Avoid hyperextending the neck during resuscitation. Proper head positioning is crucial for opening the airway and effective bag ventilation. 6. If air escapes from the mask during ventilation, improve the seal. The most common leak occurs between the nose and cheeks. Ensure the mask is the correct size and properly positioned. 7. After resuscitation, infants are at risk of deterioration even after vital signs normalize. Once adequate ventilation and circulation are established, stop ventilation and return the infant to the mother for skin-to-skin contact as soon as possible. Monitor closely for breathing difficulties, signs of asphyxia, and the need for further care. 8. Discontinue resuscitation if the infant is not breathing and has no detectable heartbeat after 10 minutes of effective resuscitation efforts. If spontaneous breathing does not occur and the heart rate remains below 60 beats per minute after 20 minutes, stop active resuscitation. Document the event and explain to the parents that the infant has died, offering them the opportunity to hold the infant if they wish. 9. Routine care for all newborns includes keeping the baby in skin-to-skin contact with the mother in a warm, draft-free room. Initiate breastfeeding within the first hour when the baby shows readiness. Allow the infant to breastfeed on demand if able to suck. Administer intramuscular vitamin K to all newborns and keep the umbilical cord clean and dry. Apply prophylactic eye ointment (e.g., tetracycline) and administer oral polio, hepatitis B, and BCG vaccines as per national guidelines. 10. For neonates with documented infection risk factors (e.g., prolonged membrane rupture, maternal fever, or foul-smelling amniotic fluid), administer intramuscular or intravenous ampicillin and gentamicin for at least two days, reassessing for signs of sepsis or positive blood cultures. Prevent hospital-acquired infections through exclusive breastfeeding, strict hand hygiene, and kangaroo mother care. Avoid incubators for preterm infants unless necessary, ensuring they are thoroughly cleaned and free of water for humidification. 11. Hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy (HIE) results from oxygen deprivation to vital organs before, during, or immediately after birth. Treat convulsions with phenobarbital, ensuring hypoglycemia is not present. Resuscitate apnea with bag and mask ventilation and manage with oxygen via nasal prongs. Feed infants unable to suck with expressed breast milk via a nasogastric tube, avoiding delayed stomach emptying to prevent regurgitation. 12. Prognosis for infants with poor motor tone (floppy or spastic) depends on recovery of motor function and sucking ability. Infants who remain floppy, spastic, unresponsive, and unable to suck within a week of birth likely have severe brain injury and poor outcomes. Discuss the situation sensitively with parents throughout the hospital stay. 13. Danger signs in neonates and young infants include drowsiness, lethargy, unconsciousness, convulsions, bulging fontanelle, irritability, and high-pitched crying. Stabilize the infant and prevent deterioration by maintaining the airway, providing oxygen if hypoxemic, and initiating bag and mask ventilation if necessary. Insert a venous cannula and administer antibiotics (ampicillin and gentamicin). Check blood glucose levels and treat hypoglycemia with intravenous glucose. 14. Treat neonatal convulsions with phenobarbital (loading dose of 20 mg/kg IV). If seizures persist, administer additional doses up to a maximum of 40 mg/kg, monitoring for apnea. Continue maintenance phenobarbital at 5 mg/kg per day if needed. Address hypocalcemia with slow IV infusion of calcium gluconate and oral supplementation. 15. For serious bacterial infections, administer first-line antibiotics (ampicillin and gentamicin) for 7–10 days. If the infant does not improve within 2–3 days, adjust antibiotic treatment or refer for further management. Perform a lumbar puncture to confirm the diagnosis of meningitis, ideally within two hours of initiating antibiotics. 16. Maintain a thermal environment by keeping the infant dry, well-wrapped, and in skin-to-skin contact with the mother (kangaroo mother care). Use external heating devices if necessary. Avoid chilling the infant during examinations or procedures. 17. Encourage frequent breastfeeding to prevent hypoglycemia. If the infant cannot feed, provide expressed breast milk via a nasogastric tube. Monitor fluid intake carefully, increasing the total volume over the first 3–5 days. Avoid overhydration with IV fluids, limiting to 100 ml/kg per day unless the infant is dehydrated or under phototherapy. 18. Use a pulse oximeter to guide oxygen therapy, maintaining oxygen saturation above 90%. Discontinue oxygen once the infant can sustain saturation above 90% in room air.
